content.title: About
content.content: Croutons are toasted pieces of bread, usually baked or fried until golden and crunchy. They can be made from any type of bread and are often seasoned with oil, herbs, or spices, giving them a flavorful, crisp texture. Croutons are commonly used as a snack, garnish for salads, soups, and sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Croutons originated in medieval Europe as a way to preserve stale bread.
There are many varieties: garlic, cheese, herb‑infused, or sweet versions with cinnamon and sugar.
In Italy similar pieces are called “crostini,” while in France they are known as “croûtons.”
Croutons can be made from white, whole‑grain, or rye bread.
In some cuisines croutons are served with aioli or used as breadcrumbs in casseroles.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Croutons provide quickly digestible carbs that supply energy.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: When made from whole‑grain bread, croutons can contribute dietary fiber, supporting digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The bread base supplies B1, B2, and niacin, which are important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Croutons may provide iron, magnesium, and phosphorus, especially if the bread is fortified.

items.title: Enhances meals
items.content: The crunchy texture adds sensory appeal to dishes, encouraging more balanced eating.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Croutons are often salted; excessive sodium intake can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Because oil is used in preparation, croutons can be calorie‑dense and should be eaten in moderation.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Croutons made from wheat bread contain gluten and are unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Trans fats
items.content: Repeated frying of oil can create trans fats, which are best avoided.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Croutons can be enjoyed as a snack, tossed into salads, soups, stews, or used as a coating for meat and fish. They also pair well with dips such as hummus or guacamole.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store croutons in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the oil from going rancid.
